game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Much less a game than an interactive story. It's a slim game with few objectives and a lot of fluff around it. The game tends to cram exposition into everything, and doesn't allow you to skip or fast-forward any of it. Utimately, while the plot is about making a god of machines, it doesn't justify its deus ex machina storytelling.

[h1]Show, Don't Tell[/h1]
I do not know who's idea it was to not allow the player to fast-forward or skip dialogue, but it was a [b]terrible[/b] decision. The sheer amount of exposition and meaningless chatter in the game is astounding. And this isn't a once or twice occurance, it's a regularly reoccuring situation where key bits of info required to advance the plot sit behind a 4 or 5 minute long unskippable dialogue sequence. And that 10+ minute bit right before the end of the game, who thought that was a good idea? And does the "administrator" need to say something every time I upload a piece of relevant info? It's like having Clippy from MS Word permanently built into the game.

Furthermore, the level of hand-holding is ridiculous. First off, for a game about parsing and collecting information, there's very little you actually have to read. The game essentially takes a big neon highlighter and highlights every single thing that might be of importance. Then, they go ahead and show you exactly where you might've missed a clue or hint. Secondly, the game has these "pivotal" moments where you have to decide which one of multiple conflicting statements is true, except that the system highlights conflicts before you even discover them. It's such a self-defeating mechanism. Imagine if the Sherlock novels had Watson discover a false clue and Sherlock responding "But Watson, that can't be the real clue cause I'm going to find the real clue on page 86!"

And if the story was entralling, and the world-building was coherent, maybe those bad gameplay elements could be overlooked. But they aren't. The plot is cheesy and the writing is lazy. How many times do you plan on having a random character with no background conveniently appear to tie-up some loose ends and then disappear forever? It's honestly kind of amazing how a game where everything you do is character building manages to have some of the most one-dimensional characters I've ever seen.

[h1]Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Chapter Select:[/b] Thanks for at least not making me have to replay the whole game to get an achievement.
[/olist]
[b]Cons[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Don't stop users from fast-forwarding text.[/b]
    [*][b]Narrative, not Narrate:[/b] I should be able to tell when I come across an important piece of dialogue. I don't need the game to highlight it a bright color, the music to change to be all dramatic, and Clippy at the top exclaiming, "Wow! That piece of dialogue sure seems important!" *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge*
[/olist]
[b]Score[/b]: 2/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Disappointing.  

1. Incredibly short.  I was surprised when it was over, as it felt like I just completed a tutorial.
2. Hand holding the entire way through.  Your "adviser" or "controller" does just that, controls you.  All you do is drag and drop things.  You make very few decisions and are spoon fed what you need to do next.
3. Worse than number 2, you are spoon fed what to think and make of your findings.  Rather than allowing you to actually investigate and figure things out, the game tells you precisely what to think.  This kills immersion and makes you, not an investigator, but just a peon dragging and dropping lines of text.
4. Game locked up for me on conclusion.  I have only played through one ending and have no desire to do the others, because the gameplay is like a tutorial from start to finish.  It would be tedious as hell playing through it again.
5. Writing is corny.  It feels like it is forcing the dialogue to be edgy and using memes.  Seriously feels like an awful episode of BBT.

So much potential, but fails the entire way through.  Definitely not worth 10 pounds.  Not even worth 5.  Maybe 1.99.  The game is incredibly short.  Steam says I played it for 7.1 hours, but the reality is I fell asleep while playing about halfway through and dozed off for a couple hours.  Even at 7 hours, the gameplay is disappointingly short.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell holds your hand so firmly throughout the entirety of the experience that it is almost hard to call it a game. The 1st mission you are given gives you hope of a grand experience of cyber sleuthing where you trawl through the lives of unaware citizens of the nation flagged up by your partner.  Then, you get to the rest of the game and realise that everything is still gloriously highlighted for you and that your only real task is ignoring irrelevant data and every now and then making a decision on certain conflicting datapoints.  It is the height of tedium and only the slow reveal the various charachters and their lives gives this any meaning.
This game tries to do the slow curtain pull that Horizon Zero Dawn did with absolutely none of the charm or charisma of that game.  2hrs in and along with my chances of a refund circling the drain is my level of interest in the conclusion of the story.  I will not come back to finish this none game, this thing that cannot even be described as a jigsaw given that not only are all the pieces highlighted for you, they are then put in place for you.  What is the point?
Orwell is yet another title that has all the potential in the world and delivers on none of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pitched as a mystery/investigation game, but really it's a glorified Visual Novel - rather than actually doing any of the investigating/hacking promised in the description, you're spoon-fed a linear progression of information. You have some agency on which to hand in, but only pre-selected bits, and most are necessary to progress. 

Buy it if you're looking for a mostly linear narrative, not if you're actually looking to play a detective game.

The adviser/tutorial character is also annoying and keeps popping up to comment on things and hold your hand. I wish they would just let me play the game and figure things out on my own.

review_text_raw:
There really should be a "maybe" option for steam reviews... Orwell is a decent game, just not the kind of game that is engaging for me.

Orwell is more a graphic adventure game rather than the espionage game it was advertised as. If you like Life is Strange, you'd probably like Orwell. 
Sadly this is not my cup of tea. I want to actually think and *play* a game. If I want a story I'd watch a movie or a let's play... The story had to be deeper than this for me to be interested.

Orwell did a good job at designing the user interface. It's beautiful, functional, and believable. The artstyle is unique and pleasing to the eye.
You'd find that despite the handholding, you will have to make choices that will have separate story outcomes. Some choices are more "right" than others, There're be hints in the game to help you make the right choice, so the choices are at least not just random.

The bad:
However, just like the other reviewers had pointed out, the articles and character profiles are too simplistic, it doesn't feel "real" enough. This design choice is understandable since adding fluff and pointless information just for the sake of making the sites "real" doesn't help with immersion either. What would help with immersion is the compelling content; which I find sadly lacking here... I find myself just skimming through for highlights. It's too much hand-holding for my taste. Really, they could have made it so much better by just making the relevant text unhighlighted so we have to actually spend effort reading and playing the game as "intended".

review_text_raw:
[h1]Thoughts[/h1]

So let start off with saying I purchased the full game after playing the demo, looking back the demo actually offers everything that you would find in the main game so I would highly suggest playing the demo before making a purchase and understand that the gameplay isnt any different.

The premise of the game is to locate pertinent information about certain suspects in response to a terror attack, the information is uploaded to a system for your superior to review. The superior talks to pretty much every time you upload something, questioning the information and how it can be used against them.  The communication is totally one way and unfortunately because of the limited information you can upload sometimes it is taken very much out of context. e.g. someone was torturing someone else with muffins…. Uploading this to the system and the superior freaked out saying this person needs investigating because they like to torture people.  Hmm, I get that is the game design but yeah it’s a bit bizarre.

I use the term locate here very loosely because the game essentially spoon feeds you documents, links and webpages that contains the important information, the task at hand is to determine if the information is actually useful or not.  Every now and then you get some information which conflicts and you have to upload just one piece of information however this type of interaction doesn’t happen that often which is a shame.

I also didn’t like how the story abruptly ended, it wasn’t obvious in any way that if I upload this bit of information the game would finish.  I was taken completely by surprise and I understand there are multiple endings available but the choice just wasn’t obvious.

Despite playing the demo I still assumed the game would offer a lot more detective work later on, I assumed that I would need to locate web pages, search people and scan the documents but no.  The system finds everything and then sends you it gift tied in a little star shaped parcel.  All you do is drag and drop blue text to the box on the left and occasionally choose between one bit of yellow text and another bit of yellow text.

Overall I think this game offers great potential but it falls down with its boring repetitive gameplay that require zero thought or analysis.  If you are wanting a detective text based game look at Hacknet, for me that that is far superior to this as its on you to find and locate the information rather than it being spoon fed to you.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is so-so; I want to recommend something *like* Orwell, but I'm on the fence about recommending Orwell itself. The game raises interesting issues, and the world would indeed be better off if everyone had at least the simulated experience of working with a large-scale surveillance system. I even usually found the story compelling, and I finished the game. However, the execution also felt a little disappointing.

The main gameplay problem, in my experience, was that sometimes I felt forced to take random or stupid-seeming actions just to see what it was that would finally advance the plot. This was in spite of the "handholding" cues the game uses to help you along.

Another thing that bothered me was a set of accuracy/realism concerns, which I will go on about below.

*************************************************

(Optional section about accuracy)

My main objection is that the game gives a poor sense of what doing an investigation with help of an Orwell-like system would actually be like in real life. In real life, either A) the computer would be a very powerful autonomous system and would make conclusions without human or involvement; or B) the human researcher would have sensible basic capabilities such as updating information, correcting machine-extracted snippets, and supplementing files with written analysis. The game tries to be somewhere in between, and in the process makes something that's unrealistic and sometimes annoying.  Also, there were also moments of "what the heck does the game want from me now", when I would add pointless or even incorrect information to the Orwell database solely to see if it would finally be the thing to move the plot forward.

The fact that you can't modify information in the Orwell crime database is pretty stupid on the face of things. To be fair, though, maybe it stands metaphorically for problems that could actually arise. For example, if two government agencies had a file on you, but the two were not in sync, the fact that you're not actually a criminal could be updated in one department's file without the second department learning about this, and perhaps the second database could lead to your extrajudicial killing.

The contextless, overaly literal way that information is passed from investigator to police is completely absurd. Perhaps this is a useful reflection of one possible way that an agency using an Orwell-type system could be dysfunctionally structured, though you'd hope that a bureaucracy wouldn't be quite that stupid. Or perhaps this limited information passing is symbolic of a potentially problem where two crime databases were linked, but could only communicate back and forth using a limited, contextless technical vocabulary, which would perpetuate misunderstanding. 

Perhaps the point of the game, though, is not to be right about the *particulars* of what could go wrong in a mass surveillance system, but more to give people an accessible experience that gives a general sense of creepiness.

[spoiler] There are 3 bombings and you have to figure out who did it. Seems intresting? WRONG! You are spoonfed this woman who hapens to be a part of this group. Then you drag and drop some info, find out some members and then it turns out they did it. There is no thought needed for the story.[/spoiler]
